analysis.one_liner: Bars all governments from requiring handguns to have loaded-chamber indicators, magazine safeties, or shell-casing microstamping.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for federal, state, or local governments to require handguns to include three safety features: an indicator showing whether the gun is loaded, a mechanism that stops it from firing when the magazine is not fully inserted, and microstamping, which etches identifying information onto shell casings when fired. States like California currently require some of these features before a handgun can be sold there. The bill would wipe out those state requirements nationwide and stop any new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Handgun manufacturers gain the most: they would never have to add safety features or microstamping equipment that state laws can currently demand as a condition of sale. Gun owners in states with strict handgun rules would face fewer purchase restrictions. Gun-rights groups would gain a federal floor that blocks states from tightening handgun design rules in the future.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal, state, or local law from requiring handguns to have a device showing whether the gun is loaded, a mechanism preventing firing without a fully inserted magazine, or microstamping of shell casings [S2].
Also blocks requirements for any technology designed to perform those functions, or that could readily be converted to do so, foreclosing future state safety mandates [S2].
Applies to handguns shipped or transported in interstate commerce, which covers essentially all handguns sold in the United States [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Residents of states that want to require these safety features lose the ability to demand them. Police and crime-lab investigators lose microstamping, a tool meant to link shell casings found at crime scenes to specific guns. Communities affected by gun violence would forgo features intended to reduce accidental shootings and aid investigations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of states with handgun safety rules

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue the bill prevents a patchwork of state rules and that some required technologies are impractical; the bill's own title frames the required features as absent from firearms 'in common use' [S2].
The bill removes state authority outright rather than phasing requirements in, so states that have already built purchase rules around these features would see them preempted [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that microstamping and loaded-chamber indicators exist to solve real problems — tracing crime guns and preventing accidental discharges — and this bill forecloses states from addressing those problems through handgun design requirements [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For manufacturers and many gun owners, the bill removes compliance costs and purchase hurdles. For people living in states that chose to require these features, the cost is the loss of a safety tool their state legislatures adopted, and the bill would also lock in that outcome against future state decisions. The bill contains no compensation or alternative safety measures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator James Risch introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, with 12 Republican co-sponsors; all 13 sponsors were Republicans [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S4].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun manufacturers and gun owners are no worse off, and states with handgun safety-feature requirements keep their rules intact because the bill never advanced. Nobody's state rules changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States with safety rules; manufacturers unchanged

industries.note: The bill would exempt manufacturers from state requirements to add loaded-chamber indicators, magazine safeties, or microstamping equipment, avoiding the engineering and tooling costs those mandates create. The public cost is the loss of safety features states chose to require. This is the industry whose products the bill shields.
Retailers in states with approved-handgun rosters tied to safety features would gain a larger, less-restricted product menu. State attorney general enforcement of design rules would be preempted.

industries.industry: State law enforcement and crime labs
industries.note: Microstamping is promoted as a forensic tool linking shell casings to specific guns; the bill would bar states from requiring the capability, foreclosing that investigative aid.
